intro.heading: You know the check was done. Can you show it?
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A registered manager is asked to show the right to work check for a carer who joined a year and a half ago. She knows it was done, because she did it. The scan sits in a shared drive under a file name nobody remembers. The reference number is on a spreadsheet. The expiry date is in a diary that belongs to someone on leave. Twenty minutes later she has found most of it. Nothing was missing in the end. The trouble was that nothing was in one place, and the inspector watched her look.

trail.text: The manager carries out the right to work check at the interview.
She scans the document and saves it in the shared drive.
She notes the reference on the staff spreadsheet.
The folder is renamed and the scan moves with it.
A colleague updates the spreadsheet but not the scan.
Nobody can say which version is the current one.
The date to look at the check again has passed unseen.
"Show me the right to work check for this carer."

trail_close: The check was done properly. What was missing was one place to hold the document and the record together. Here is how a register does that.

talk.heading: Questions managers ask about holding the check
talk.sub: Read this as a conversation. These are the questions we hear most.

items.q: Does CareStream carry out the right to work check for us?
items.a: No. The check is the employer's responsibility, and the GOV.UK employer's guide sets out how to do it. CareStream records what you did, holds the document and reminds you of dates.

items.q: Which documents can we upload?
items.a: Any staff credential on the register can have a file: DBS, right to work, passport, professional registration, references, and the extra documents for visas, driving and contracts.

items.q: Who can see the documents?
items.a: Admins only. The register is not shown to staff, and staff cannot upload their own.

items.q: What if a document is missing?
items.a: The entry shows as missing, and the View button does not appear, so it is easy to spot and chase.

items.q: Will it warn me before a date runs out?
items.a: Yes. Entries turn to expiring within 30 days, and the daily digest email to admins covers expiring and expired items.

items.q: Does this prove we are compliant?
items.a: No. It shows what you hold and when it ends. Whether the service meets the regulations is judged by the Care Quality Commission, not by a register.

items.q: Which plan has the register?
items.a: The Enterprise plan. Look at the pricing page for the current details.

items.q: Can we try it first?

cards.title: It does not do the check
cards.body: The register records and reminds. Right to work and DBS checks remain the employer's responsibility, and CareStream does not advise on a legal outcome.

cards.title: It does not verify a document is genuine

faqs.heading: Right to work checks and staff files, answered

groups.group: About the check and the record

items.q: What should we keep as evidence of a right to work check?
items.a: Follow the GOV.UK employer's guide, which explains how to carry out the checks and which documents are acceptable. CareStream stores the document you upload and the details you record.

items.q: Do we need to check again later?
items.a: For some workers a follow up check is needed. The GOV.UK guide explains when. If a time limit applies, set the date on the register and it will warn you 30 days ahead.

items.q: What does Regulation 19 say about staff records?
items.a: Regulation 19 requires that persons employed are of good character, have the skills they need and are fit for the work, and that recruitment procedures are operated effectively. Schedule 3 lists the information that must be available, and it includes proof of identity with a recent photograph.

items.q: What does the View button do?
items.a: It opens the uploaded document in a window over the register, next to the reference number, dates, notes and status, so you can check the file against what is recorded.

items.q: Can staff upload their own right to work document?
items.a: No. The register is admin only, and admins upload the documents.

items.q: Is it a DBS tracker as well?
items.a: Yes. DBS sits on the same register as right to work, registration and references, each with dates, a file and a status.

items.q: Is a scan as good as the original?
items.a: That depends on the check you carried out. The GOV.UK employer's guide sets out what the employer must do and what to keep, so follow it. CareStream holds what you upload.

items.q: Should every document go on the register?
items.a: Hold what your recruitment policy says you rely on. The register has places for DBS, right to work, passport, professional registration and references, and for extras where they apply.

items.q: What if the file we uploaded is the wrong one?
items.a: Upload the right file and check the record against it. The point of the View window is to catch exactly this, by putting the document beside what you recorded.

guide.heading: Keeping a staff file you can stand behind
guide.lede: A good file is simple. The document, the record and the next date, all in the same place.

paragraphs: Record it the same day, while the document is on the desk. Upload the file then, not at the end of the week, because "later" is where scans go missing.
checklist: Record the reference, issue date and expiry date
Upload the document at the same time
Add a note if anything is unusual
Set a date to look at the check again where one applies

sections.h3: When you look at the register
paragraphs: Choose a regular moment, such as the first Monday of each quarter, and use it. Open a handful of documents at random and compare them with the record.
If something has changed, update the record and the file together so they cannot drift.
checklist: Look for expired and expiring entries
Open a sample of documents with View
Chase anything missing
Write down what you changed

sections.h3: Answering the inspector on the day
paragraphs: Inspectors ask for evidence in many shapes, and a staff file is one of the commonest. They may pick a name from your rota and ask to see what you hold. What they want is a document that matches the record, and an answer that does not depend on who is in the building.

Practise it once. Choose a member of staff at random, find the right to work check, open the document, read out the reference and dates, and see how long it took. If it took more than a minute, find out where the time went and fix that first.
checklist: Pick a name at random each quarter
Open the document with View
Read the reference and dates aloud
Time it and note what slowed you down

guide.note: Every example here is illustrative. It is not legal advice, and the employer remains responsible for right to work and DBS checks.

intro.heading: Every nurse's registration needs a date someone is watching.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: The deputy manager of a nursing home keeps a list of nurses and their revalidation dates in the back of a notebook. When she moves to another service, the notebook goes with her. Three weeks later the new deputy is asked, in passing, how many nurses are due to revalidate in the next quarter. Nobody knows. Everyone is registered, as it turns out. But for a few days nobody could say so with confidence, and that is a worse position to be in than it sounds.

trail.text: A nurse joins and her registration is checked on the register.
Her PIN is written in the staff file.
Her certificate is filed in a folder.
The revalidation date is in the deputy's notebook.
The deputy leaves and the notebook goes with her.
Nobody is watching the date.
The nurse is busy and has not mentioned it.
"Can you show me that your nurses are all registered?"

trail_close: The registration was real. What was missing was a date in a place everyone could see. Here is how the register holds it.

why.heading: A registration is a standing question, not a one off answer.

cards.title: A lapse is hard to see late

talk.heading: Questions managers ask about registered staff

items.q: Does CareStream check the NMC register for us?
items.a: No. It holds what you enter. Looking someone up on the professional register is still a manual task. What changes is that the date and the certificate are in one place and you are warned before a date arrives.

items.q: Which bodies can we record?
items.a: NMC, GPhC, HCPC, GMC and Social Work England, plus Other for anything else.

items.q: What is the NMC PIN?
items.a: It is the registration number the NMC gives each registrant. Record it as the number against the person and keep your own record of when you last checked it.

items.q: Will we be reminded about revalidation?
items.a: Yes. Set the renewal or revalidation date, and the entry turns to expiring 30 days before it. The daily digest email to admins covers it.

items.q: Who sees this?
items.a: Admins only. Staff do not see the register.

items.q: Can we use it for non nursing staff?
items.a: Yes, for any role where you hold a professional registration, such as pharmacists, therapists or social workers.

items.q: Does it replace our own registration checks?
items.a: No. Registration checks are the employer's responsibility. The register records them and reminds you.

items.q: Which plan is it on?
items.a: The Enterprise plan. You can book a demo to see it.

cards.title: It does not look people up
cards.body: CareStream does not query the NMC or any other register. You check, and you record.

cards.title: It does not decide whether someone can practise
cards.body: Registration status is for the professional body and the employer. The register holds your record of it.

cards.title: It is not a revalidation tool for the nurse
cards.body: Staff do not see or use the register. Revalidation itself is done by the nurse with the NMC.

faqs.heading: Registered staff and the register, answered

items.q: How do we keep track of nurse revalidation dates?
items.a: Record the revalidation date against each nurse on the workforce register. It shows as valid, expiring within 30 days or expired, and admins get a daily digest email. The NMC explains revalidation on its own site.

items.q: Can we record HCPC and GMC registration too?
items.a: Yes. You choose the body from a list that includes the HCPC, GMC, GPhC and Social Work England, and add Other for anything else.

items.q: What should we keep for each registered member of staff?
items.a: The registration number, a copy of the certificate and the date to check again. Regulation 19 says recruitment procedures must be operated effectively, and the regulation is worth reading in full.

items.q: Does CareStream run an NMC PIN check?
items.a: No. The register records the PIN you enter and the dates. The check itself is yours.

items.q: Who can see registration details?
items.a: Admins only.

items.q: Can staff upload their own certificate?
items.a: No. Admins upload it.

items.q: Should the register hold agency nurses?
items.a: No. Agency workers are held by their agency and are left out of the register.

items.q: How early should we start asking about revalidation?
items.a: There is no fixed rule for the service. The register warns you 30 days before a date, and many managers start the conversation earlier, in supervision.

items.q: Is this a replacement for our own checks of the professional register?
items.a: No. You still check the body's own register. The workforce register keeps your record, the certificate and the date to look again.

items.q: Does the register show conditions or restrictions on a registration?
items.a: It holds the notes you add. If the professional body shows a condition, record it in the notes and handle it under your own policy.

items.q: What counts as a registered role in a care home?
items.a: That depends on the service. Nursing homes rely on registered nurses, and some services also employ therapists, pharmacists or social workers. Record the body for each.

items.q: Can we hold a nursing associate here?
items.a: The body list covers the NMC, and you can record the number and dates in the same way. Use Other if a body is not listed.

guide.heading: A simple routine for registered staff
guide.lede: The routine is short, and it works because it is regular.

paragraphs: Check the registration on the professional body's own register and record what you saw, with the number and the date. Upload the certificate straight away.
checklist: Check the body's own register
Record the number and the date you checked
Upload the certificate
Set the next date to look

paragraphs: Look at the dates for registered staff on the register. Check anything expiring in the next two months with the person, not just on screen.
checklist: Look for expiring and expired entries
Talk to anyone due soon
Check again on the body's register
Update the record and file together

paragraphs: An expiring entry is a prompt to talk, not a verdict on anyone. Speak to the nurse early, ask how revalidation is going and whether they need anything from you, such as time to complete reflective accounts or a discussion. The professional body sets what a person must do. The service can make it easier.

Write down what you agreed and when you will look again. If a registration does lapse, the actions that follow depend on your policy and your own professional advice, and are not something the register decides.
checklist: Speak to the person early
Ask what support they need
Record what you agreed
Set the next date to look

sections.h3: What to put in the notes
paragraphs: The notes field is where the context lives. Record when you last looked at the professional body's own register, who looked, and anything the nurse told you about their revalidation. A short line such as "checked, no conditions, date confirmed at supervision" does more good in an inspector's hands than a blank box.
Keep notes factual and brief. They are part of a staff record, so write what you would be content for the person to read.
checklist: Date you last checked the body's register
Who checked
Anything the person told you
Date of the next check

intro.heading: Some documents belong to a few people. Those are the easy ones to lose.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A home care manager has forty carers. Six are sponsored workers with a time limit on their right to work, and fifteen drive their own cars between visits. Their paperwork lives in different places, because the standard staff checklist has no row for a sponsorship end date or an MOT. A sponsored carer's end date passes quietly in the month the manager is covering a rota gap. A driver's insurance lapses in the same quarter. Both are found by chance. The standard list was fine. It just did not know about the exceptions.

trail.text: A carer joins on a visa with a time limited right to work.
The manager records the right to work check as usual.
A second carer is added who uses her own car for visits.
The licence and insurance are copied into a folder.
The standard checklist has no row for a sponsorship end date.
The MOT on a staff car runs out unnoticed.
A sponsorship end date passes during a busy week.
"How do you track documents that only some staff hold?"

trail_close: The checks were sound. The gap was a place for the documents that only some people need. Here is how the register covers them.

cards.title: Some dates carry real weight

talk.heading: Questions managers ask about visas and driving

items.q: Does CareStream know the rules on sponsorship?
items.a: No. It records the end date you enter and warns you before it arrives. Sponsorship duties and right to work checks are the employer's responsibility, and the GOV.UK employer's guide is the place to read them.

items.q: Will my British staff show as missing a visa?
items.a: No. These extra documents are never marked as missing. They only appear for the staff who have one.

items.q: Which driving documents can we hold?
items.a: Driving licence, business use insurance and MOT.

items.q: Can we check the licence itself?
items.a: The register holds the document and the dates. A licence holder can share their licence details through GOV.UK, and checking is your task.

items.q: Do the alerts cover these documents?
items.a: Yes. The daily digest email to admins includes them, and a visa whose sponsorship is ending is included.

items.q: Are these staff visible to other staff?
items.a: No. The register is for admins only.

items.q: What about agency workers?
items.a: Agency workers are held by their agency and are left out of the register.

items.q: Which plan?
items.a: The Enterprise plan. You can book a demo.

cards.title: It does not advise on sponsorship
cards.body: CareStream is not an immigration or sponsorship adviser. It records dates and documents you enter.

cards.title: It does not check licences or insurance
cards.body: Verification stays with you. The register holds the evidence and the date.

cards.title: It does not manage vehicles or mileage
cards.body: There is no mileage, fleet or expenses feature. It simply keeps the documents.

items.q: How do we track a care worker visa end date?
items.a: Add the visa on the workforce register with the sponsorship end date, and upload the document. The entry will turn to expiring 30 days before and the daily admin digest will include it.

items.q: Does CareStream manage our sponsorship licence?
items.a: No. It does not manage a sponsorship licence or give immigration advice. It holds the documents and dates for each person.

items.q: Do we need to do follow up right to work checks?
items.a: The GOV.UK employer's guide explains when follow up checks are needed. Record the check and its date on the register.

items.q: How do we handle staff who use their own cars for work?
items.a: Hold the driving licence, business use insurance and MOT on the register for the staff who drive, each with dates and a file. Grey fleet policy itself is for you and your insurer to settle.

items.q: Why are these documents never marked missing?
items.a: Because they only apply to some staff. A carer who does not drive has no entry, so nothing shows as missing.

items.q: Who sees these documents?
items.a: Admins only.

items.q: Can we hold a passport as well?
items.a: Yes. Passport is one of the credentials on the register, along with DBS, right to work, professional registration and references.

items.q: What if a driver changes cars?
items.a: Record the new insurance and MOT details and upload the new documents, so the register shows what is current for that person.

items.q: Do sponsored workers appear differently on the register?
items.a: They have a visa entry with a sponsorship end date in the Also held column. Staff without one have no entry and are never marked missing.

items.q: Is the grey fleet our responsibility?
items.a: A service that lets staff use their own vehicles for work will usually want its policy, and its insurer, to say what is required. CareStream holds the documents and dates you decide you need.

items.q: Do we need business use insurance for every driver?
items.a: That is for your policy and your insurer. The register simply holds the document where you hold one.

items.q: Can we see all sponsored workers in one place?
items.a: Visa entries sit in the Also held column on the register, so you can see them beside each person's other documents.

intro.heading: The form exists. The question is whether you can find it, and whether it is right.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: On a quiet Sunday a carer feels unwell and is taken to hospital by ambulance. The senior on duty remembers there is a form for this. It is in a folder in the office, in a drawer that is locked, and the key is with the manager who is away. Eventually someone finds a phone number on an old rota. It turns out to belong to a partner who has since moved. Nobody did anything wrong. The form was completed on day one and never looked at again, and that is how most of them end up.

trail.text: A new carer fills in an emergency contact form on paper.
It goes into her staff file in the office.
The file is put in a locked drawer.
Her partner changes number and she forgets to say.
A rota is photocopied with her old number on it.
The key holder is on leave.
She is taken ill on a Sunday shift.
Nobody can find a number that works.

trail_close: The form was done properly. The gap was an up to date record that an admin could open from anywhere, and a way to see who has nothing recorded. Here is how the register does it.

why.heading: Emergency details are only useful if they are right.

faqs.heading: Emergency contacts and staff records, answered

items.q: What should an emergency contact form include?
items.a: At least a name, relationship and a phone number, and a second number where you can. CareStream holds an emergency contact and a next of kin, and lets you mark them as the same person.

items.q: How often should we check emergency contact details?
items.a: There is no set rule, so choose a rhythm you can keep, such as at each supervision. Record the change and the Personal column updates.

items.q: Is next of kin the same as an emergency contact?
items.a: Not always. Someone may want a friend rung first and a relative recorded as next of kin. The register holds both and has a shortcut for when they are the same.

items.q: Who can see staff personal details?
items.a: Admins only.

items.q: Can we see who has not filled in their details?
items.a: Yes. The Personal column shows how many of five sections are complete for each person.

items.q: Does the register store anything about health?
items.a: No. It holds date of birth, emergency contact and next of kin only.

items.q: Should we ask for health information here?
items.a: The register does not hold health information. It holds date of birth, emergency contact and next of kin. Health matters belong in the right place under your own policy.

items.q: Can an emergency contact be someone who is not a relative?
items.a: Yes. It can be anyone the person wants called. Next of kin can be recorded separately, or marked as the same.

items.q: What if a person does not want to give details?
items.a: Record that they declined, in your own notes, and revisit it at supervision. The Personal column will show the gap, which is a prompt to ask again kindly.

items.q: Can we record two emergency contacts?
items.a: The register holds an emergency contact and a next of kin. Use the next of kin entry for a second person where they differ.

items.q: What if someone has no next of kin?
items.a: Record what they tell you and note it. Some people have no family close by, and a friend or neighbour is a perfectly good emergency contact.

items.q: How do I know a number is right?
items.a: Ask the person to read it back when you enter it, and again at supervision. The register can only hold what it is told.

items.q: Is an emergency contact a legal requirement for a staff file?
items.a: Schedule 3 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 lists the information that must be available for each person employed, and an emergency contact is not on that list. Holding one is good practice and a matter for your own policy. Regulation 19 covers recruitment procedures in general.

The contract is in a file, the hours are on a rota, the holiday year starts in April for some staff and on the anniversary for others. A simple question takes three places to answer. It is not a dispute. It is only a delay, and it comes round every time someone asks.

items.q: How much holiday are care staff entitled to?
items.a: GOV.UK explains that most workers are legally entitled to 5.6 weeks of paid holiday a year, including agency workers and those with irregular hours. Your contracts may give more. CareStream records the entitlement you set.

items.q: Do zero hours staff get holiday?
items.a: The GOV.UK holiday guidance covers workers with irregular hours, so read it for the detail. CareStream lets you record a zero hours contract type and an entitlement in days or hours.

items.q: What is a probation period?
items.a: A set time at the start of a job when the employer reviews whether the person is right for the role. CareStream records the end date so you can plan the review.

items.q: Can we book leave in CareStream?
items.a: No. It records entitlement only.

items.q: Who can see the Contract and holiday tab?

items.q: How long can a probation period be?

items.q: Can we hold a bank worker's contract here?

items.a: Entitlement usually follows the contract and the hours, so it can differ. Record what each contract says, in days or hours, and use GOV.UK for the statutory baseline.

items.a: Yes. The email goes to any member of staff on the register with a date of birth entered by an admin, whatever shift they work.

items.q: Should we tell staff that we hold their birthdays?
items.a: Yes. Tell people when you collect their date of birth that it is held on an admin only tab and used for the birthday emails and nothing else, and that either email can be switched off.

items.q: Are birthday emails part of safer recruitment?
items.a: No. They are a courtesy. Regulation 19 and Schedule 3 deal with recruitment procedures and the information held on each person employed, and a birthday email is not part of either.

guide.heading: A simple birthday habit

paragraphs: A week is enough to do something modest. Decide in advance what your service does and keep it the same for everyone, so nobody is left out.
checklist: Decide your standard gesture
Buy the card at the start of the week
Ask the team to sign it
Mark the day on the handover

paragraphs: Treat each person the same, and remember that some people would rather not be made a fuss of. A quiet word can be enough.
checklist: Same gesture for everyone
Ask anyone who prefers no fuss
Include night staff and bank staff
Look at the 60 day panel monthly

paragraphs: A reminder is more useful when it leads somewhere. Agree with your senior team who does what: who buys the card, who brings the cake, who tells the night shift. When the roles are clear, a birthday takes two minutes and never lands on one person.
Keep the gesture proportionate. A signed card and a mention at handover are plenty for most teams, and the point is that it is the same for everyone.
checklist: Agree who buys the card
Agree who tells the night team
Keep the gesture proportionate
Review once a year with the team

paragraphs: Both emails are controlled in Settings, Notifications. An admin can switch the seven day reminder off, the happy birthday email off, or both,.
If you switch the happy birthday email off, nothing changes for the admin reminder, and the other way round. Choose the mix that suits your service.
checklist: Open Settings, Notifications
Decide on the admin reminder
Decide on the staff email
Tell the team what you chose

intro.heading: A list of names is not the same as knowing your team.
intro.sub: A scenario we see in many care settings.
intro.paragraph: A new registered manager takes over a home with sixty staff. In the first fortnight she is handed a spreadsheet of names, roles and document dates. It is accurate. It is also hard to use, because half the names mean nothing to her yet and the night team are people she has never met. When she sees that a name has an expiring DBS, she cannot picture who it is. She asks around. It takes ten minutes to put a face to a name, and ten minutes is a lot over a day.

trail.text: A new manager receives the staff spreadsheet.
She learns the day team and their roles.
She reads the document dates for the first time.
Night staff are still names without faces.
She sees a DBS due and cannot place the person.
Bank staff add more unfamiliar names.
She asks around to put faces to dates.
"Who is this member of staff?" and nobody is sure.

trail_close: The spreadsheet was accurate. It was just missing faces and a view of everything in one row. Here is how the register helps.

talk.heading: Questions managers ask about the register as a whole

items.q: What do the pictures do?
items.a: Staff pictures show next to each name on the register, so an admin can put a face to a name when looking at documents and dates. Book a demo to see it with example data.

items.q: Who can see the register?
items.a: Admins only. Staff never see it.

items.q: What columns does it have?
items.a: Documents with their status, a Personal column with sections filled in, and an Also held column for extras.

items.q: Is it a replacement for our HR system?
items.a: No. It is a record of documents, personal details and entitlement, with reminders. It is not payroll, rota or time and attendance.

items.q: Does it cover agency staff?
items.a: No. Agency workers are held by their agency and are not on the register.

items.q: Can we use it for a quick check before a visit?
items.a: Yes. Look for expired and expiring entries and open a few documents with View.

items.q: Does it prove we are compliant?
items.a: No. It shows what you hold. Whether you meet the regulations is for the Care Quality Commission to judge.

items.q: Which plan?
items.a: The Enterprise plan. You can book a demo.

cards.title: It is not an HR system
cards.body: There is no payroll, rota, holiday booking or performance management. It holds documents and details with reminders.

cards.title: It does not replace knowing your team
cards.body: A picture helps, but it does not replace walking the floor and talking to people.

cards.title: It is for admins only
cards.body: Staff do not see it, and they do not upload their own documents.

items.q: What is a staff register?
items.a: A list of the people who work in the service with the key details about each. CareStream's workforce register shows a picture, documents with status, personal details and extras, and is admin only.

items.q: Which documents does it hold?
items.a: DBS, right to work, passport, professional registration, references, and extras such as visas, driving documents and the contract. Regulation 19 and its Schedule 3 list the information that must be available for each person employed.

items.q: Does it replace a staff photo directory?
items.a: It shows a picture beside each name for admins. It is not a public directory and staff do not see it.

items.q: Who can see it?
items.a: Admins only.

items.q: Is it on every plan?
items.a: No. It is on the Enterprise plan.

items.q: Can we see it across several homes?
items.a: Yes, see the workforce and multi site page for how the group view works.

items.q: Does the register show training too?
items.a: Training results are in the training matrix and the staff record. The workforce register is for documents, personal details and entitlement, with reminders.

items.q: Is it only useful before an inspection?
items.a: No. It is most useful as a weekly glance. A register you look at often has fewer surprises in it than one you open before a visit.

items.q: What is the difference between this and a spreadsheet?
items.a: The documents sit behind each entry and open with View, the dates carry colours and a daily digest email, and everything is admin only. A spreadsheet can hold the same facts, but it cannot warn you.

items.q: Does the register replace an annual staff file audit?
items.a: No. It helps you run one. The HR staff files audit is a separate free check you can run alongside it.

items.q: What does a missing entry mean?
items.a: It means no document is recorded for that credential. Extras such as visas and driving documents are never marked missing for staff they do not apply to.

items.q: Can we use the register for new starters?
items.a: Yes. Adding each person's documents and details as they join gives you a complete row from the start, and the picture makes them easier for the whole management team to place.

items.q: What does the law say about staff records?
items.a: Regulation 19 of the Health and Social Care Act 2008 (Regulated Activities) Regulations 2014 says recruitment procedures must be operated effectively, and requires the information in Schedule 3 to be available for each person employed. A register helps you hold and find it. It does not decide whether you meet the regulation.

guide.heading: Using the register as a whole
guide.lede: A short routine that suits a busy manager.

paragraphs: Spend five minutes looking at expiring and expired items and the birthday panel. Small, regular looks beat a yearly clean up.
checklist: Open the register on a set day
Look for expiring and expired entries
Look at the next birthdays
Chase one thing, not everything

paragraphs: Once a quarter, open a sample of documents with View and compare them to the record. Check the Personal and Also held columns for gaps.
checklist: Open five documents with View
Check the Personal column
Check the Also held column
Note what you fixed

sections.h3: Getting the register ready for a visit
paragraphs: Before a planned visit, take twenty minutes to look at the register as an outsider would. Look at the statuses, fix what you can, and make a note of what is in hand. An honest, tidy register with items being chased reads better than a perfect one that was clearly cleaned up overnight.

Remember that the register shows what you hold. It does not tell the inspector how well you support your staff. Be ready to talk about supervision, training and how you know your team, as well as the documents.
checklist: Look at the status columns and fix what you can
Note what is in hand
Open a few documents with View
Be ready to talk about people, not just papers

sections.h3: What to look for in the columns
paragraphs: Look at the pattern, not just the single row. A column that is mostly green with a few amber entries is healthy. A column that is empty for half the team tells you a document has never been collected, which is a different job from chasing a renewal.
Do the same with the Personal column. A row with one section filled in needs a conversation, not just a click.
checklist: Look for patterns, not just rows
Separate never collected from expiring
Check the Personal column
Chase one theme at a time
